prize_parts.citation: for credible empirical analysis of how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B037 now looks to me like the strongest candidate to carry forward. It is the one with the broadest opening support, and several colleagues who disagree on much else rank it highly. On substance, the work combines a clear conceptual frame (tasks, skill demand) with transparent, design-based evidence on import competition. Its central claims are exposed to scrutiny: the shift-share designs, the pre-trends and the persistence of effects have been tested and re-tested, and the qualitative findings have been reproduced with data from other countries. That is the kind of credibility I weight most heavily. The work also has large policy relevance for how societies think about the costs of trade and automation. After reading colleagues' attribution arguments I have moved from Autor and Hanson alone to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Dorn is a core co-author of the import-shock papers, and omitting him would misstate where the empirical evidence came from. The citation is deliberately framed around the credibly identified evidence on trade and technology shocks rather than the whole skill-premium history.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B037 combines two strands that could be judged separate discoveries: the long-run skill-premium and task framework, and the China-shock evidence. A three-person cap cannot honour the task-framework authors, including Katz, Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu, who is already a laureate. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, and some magnitudes depend on specification and on the shift-share instrument. The topic is also close to the 2023 and 2024 prizes on skills, technology and inequality. If the Committee judges the framework strand to be the main discovery, this configuration under-credits it.

responses.point: Friberg proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn for B037, treating the China-shock work as the cleanest attributable core. He notes that credit for the technology strand is more diffuse and that the long-run interpretation of the shock is still contested.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and have adopted it. The ADH import-shock papers are a coherent, jointly authored body of work, and Dorn's role cannot reasonably be separated from Autor's and Hanson's. I also share Friberg's caution about long-run magnitudes. That is why my citation emphasises credible evidence on adjustment rather than a settled verdict on the size of the effects. Where I differ is that I would not drop the task and technology strand from the citation. Autor carries that credit in his own right, even if Katz and others do not appear.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B037 first. She frames the attribution choice as Dorn versus Katz, notes that Katz's contribution partly overlaps with Goldin's prize, and observes that Acemoglu shaped the task framework but is not on the credited list.
responses.response: I largely agree with her framing and take the overlap with Goldin seriously. That overlap is the main reason I favour Dorn over Katz. Katz's skill-premium work is foundational, but a committee that treated it as the anchor would be partly re-rewarding recognised territory. I would qualify her view that the two strands naturally form a single discovery. The shared theme is how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand. The identification strategies and the evidence are different, and I would want the citation worded so that it does not imply the task framework is wholly credited to the named laureates. I also agree that B038 is better treated as a possibility for later, because its causal neighbourhood-effect findings have had less time for independent replication.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B004 (Grossman and Helpman) first. He argues that protection-for-sale and the innovation-and-growth synthesis are foundational and general, and that Helpman is credited as a clear joint originator with Grossman.
responses.response: I accept that the Grossman-Helpman framework is foundational and widely used. My hesitation is that, as Hassler himself notes, the empirical support for its specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed. For me, tests that hold up weigh more than conceptual generality. The ballot description also covers only the policy strand and not the growth synthesis. If the Committee wants a trade prize, I still lean toward B008, where the core mechanisms of selection and reallocation have been checked across many countries and datasets. I recognise the real tension that Helpman appears on both ballots, and I would not credit him twice.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B025 (Kiyotaki and Moore) first as a canonical macro-finance mechanism that the 2008 crisis made relevant. He argues for restricting credit to the two originators and sees little overlap with Bernanke's work.
responses.response: The attribution to the two originators is cleaner than in most macro candidates, and I agree with that. My concern is evidentiary. The mechanism is established mainly through stylised and calibrated models, and Krusell himself acknowledges that empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is less settled than the theory. Several colleagues also flag the 2022 prize as adjacent. I would be more comfortable with B025 if someone could point to credible, direct evidence for the collateral channel beyond the post-crisis narrative. I have not seen that argued in the openings, so I leave B025 outside my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name next to Autor and Hanson, and whether the Committee would rather credit the skill-premium and task strand than the import-shock strand.

How much of the China-shock effect is robust to specification, instrument choice and long-run persistence. I have not checked the underlying papers independently and rely on my recollection of the literature.
Whether the proximity to the 2023 and 2024 prizes on skills, technology and inequality should reduce the weight given to B037.

Whether B008 would deserve priority if a trade-centred prize is preferred, given that Helpman's credit is split with B004 and that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are outside the credited names, have claims on the empirical origins.
Whether the framework in B013 can be attributed to three people without arbitrary exclusions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in behavioural and experimental economics and metascience, and my profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to the credited names on B037, B008 or B013. My general interest in replicability may make me weight robustness of evidence more than other members do. That is a perspective, not a conflict.
